route: Free search. Chosen formulation: the negative half of the all-switches/AUSO pivot read in the language of the policy-iteration literature ("binary" = two actions per state), plus an attempt to build the first superlinear all-switches family on binary stopping SSGs. Nearest anti-list item: strategy-improvement switch counts. It is not that item because (i) no round identified the project's open item (a superpolynomial all-switches family on stopping SSGs, equivalently a family defeating M3) with the published open problem "is Howard's rule exponential on 2-action MDPs?", and (ii) the mechanism attempted (a binary deceleration lane re-run by alternately rising exit/target sources, with amplification from cycles closed by consecutive switches) is absent from every family in frontier.tex. Everything claimed proved is verified in exact rational arithmetic; the literature statements are quoted, not proved.
headline: The project's missing superpolynomial all-switches family contains, as its one-player case, the published open problem "Howard's rule on 2-action MDPs" (exponential only with Theta(n) actions: Friedmann 2011, Fearnley 2010, Christ-Yannakakis 2023; linear is the best known for constant actions, per Mukherjee-Kalyanakrishnan ICAPS 2025); and a one-line corollary of cor:comparison shows why the known counters do not binarise: in a binary stopping SSG an intrinsic cycle is either being closed right now or is dead for ever, so the delayed cycle-closing (appeal competition) that times Fearnley's and Friedmann's exponential jumps has no binary analogue.

results.name: fs14:howard (identification of the one-player pivot)
results.statement: A stopping SSG with Vmin empty is literally a transient two-action reachability MDP and all-switches is Howard's greedy rule on it; hence a stopping one-player SSG family with a superpolynomial all-switches run is an exponential-type lower bound for Howard's algorithm on 2-action MDPs, and conversely any polynomial bound for Howard on 2-action transient reachability MDPs bounds the one-player all-switches run of every stopping SSG.
results.argument: Max vertex = state with two deterministic actions, average vertex = one action with probabilities 1/2,1/2, sinks absorbing; stopping makes every policy transient so total reward = reach probability = val_sigma (thm:eval-stopfree); with two actions, 'switch every state with a switchable action to its most appealing action' is exactly 'switch every strictly switchable vertex'.
results.verification: Literal restatement; the all-switches runner used below (allsw.py) was validated against brute-force wstar/profile_value on 400 random stopping games (t_allsw_check.py), including Min best response by policy iteration, which is sound only on stopping games and is asserted so.

results.name: fs14:literature (state of the art, attributed)
results.statement: Exponential all-switches lower bounds are known for parity/mean-payoff/discounted/simple stochastic games (Friedmann LMCS 2011: G_n with 10n+4 nodes, d_i has successors {s,e_i,r} u {a_j : j<2i+1}, r and s have n+1 successors, k_i has n-i+1), for Howard on total/average-reward MDPs (Fearnley ICALP 2010: b_i has 2i lane actions plus y, x, f_j, a_i; lane states d_k have three actions; timing by Proposition 4 there, appeal(b_i,a_i) < Val(b_i)+1), and for reachability MDPs (Christ-Yannakakis STOC 2023) -- all with Theta(n) actions per state. Mukherjee-Kalyanakrishnan (ICAPS 2025) state that for a constant number of actions per state the tightest lower bound for Howard's rule is linear and that 'it remains unknown if exponentially-long chains are possible for HPI on 2-action MDPs'; Hansen-Zwick 2010's Omega(n^2) is reported there to use Theta(n) actions as well. Every family in frontier.tex has all-switches length <= N, matching the state of the literature.
results.argument: Fetched Friedmann's Table 4 verbatim (ar5iv), extracted Fearnley's full text from the arXiv PDF (pdftext.py -> fearnley.txt), fetched the abstracts of Christ-Yannakakis and Mukherjee-Kalyanakrishnan.
results.verification: Quotes recorded in fs14.tex and fearnley.txt; not a mathematical claim of this route.

results.name: fs14:deadset (dead re-routings)
results.statement: G stopping, sigma any Max strategy, W a set of Max vertices none strictly switchable under val_sigma. Then val_{sigma[W]} <= val_sigma, and along any run of strictly improving switches from sigma (single or multiple, all-switches included) val_{sigma[W]} <= val_{sigma_t} for all t. Min, if present, best-responds throughout.
results.argument: T_{sigma[W]} val_sigma <= val_sigma coordinatewise (equality off W, <= on W by non-switchability), so cor:comparison gives val_{sigma[W]} <= val_sigma; the reversed computation gives val_{sigma_t[S]} >= val_{sigma_t} for any set S of strictly switchable vertices (lem:switch for |S|=1), so the run is monotone.
results.verification: t_deadset.py: 250 random stopping games (152 two-player), 1202 re-routings of up to three non-switchable vertices, each dominated by every later value vector of the all-switches run; exact rationals.

results.name: fs14:cycle (a cycle is active now or dead for ever)
results.statement: For an intrinsic cycle C of Max vertices (C-options lead to the next cycle vertex through average vertices exiting only to sinks; closed value lambda_C intrinsic): if at round t no vertex of C is strictly switchable toward C, then for all t' >= t val_{sigma_t'} >= lambda_C on C, and C is closed at t' only if it was already closed at t. Hence at every round of an all-switches run each intrinsic cycle either has a vertex switching toward it or will never be closed.
results.argument: Apply fs14:deadset with W = the cycle vertices not on C; if C first became closed at t''>t, the last vertices to enter were strictly improving switches, which strictly raise their own values (val_{sigma''}(v) = val_{sigma''}(bar sigma(v)) >= val_{sigma'}(bar sigma(v)) > val_{sigma'}(v)), contradicting lambda_C(v) = val_{sigma''}(v) > val_{sigma'}(v) >= lambda_C(v).
results.verification: t_cycle.py: 150 random games built around random intrinsic cycles of length 2-4 with random masses/pass probabilities (all dyadic), 272 (round, cycle) inactivity events, the intrinsic-value property, the lower bound and 'never closed later' all hold; exact rationals.

results.name: fs14:no-arming (interpretation, not a theorem)
results.statement: Fearnley's and Friedmann's exponential jumps are timed by postponing a switch into an already attractive cycle via a competing action of larger appeal for 2i+1 rounds; by fs14:cycle a binary game has no such state -- an attractive intrinsic cycle always has a switching vertex, an unattractive one is dead for ever -- so impedance-type amplification (thm:impedance) is available in a binary game only from the first round, never after a delay. Neither Min gates nor exact ties change this (Min caps an option at its escape value; a tie yields jump <= excess). This does not prove that no binary counter exists.
results.argument: Direct reading of fs14:cycle against Fearnley's Proposition 4 and Friedmann's cycle gates; the Min-gate and tie cases were checked by hand computation of the option values (min(g,e) caps the post-switch value; a tied loop option gains at most r*delta/(1-h) <= delta with r <= 1-h).
results.verification: Consistent with the search below; no counterexample family was found.

results.name: fs14:lane (the binary deceleration lane)
results.statement: Lane(k): Max vertices l_i -> (l_{i+1}, x_i), l_{k+1} = t1, x_i a coin of value 1 - i 2^{-b}, b = floor(log2 k)+2; N = O(k log k). From the all-exit strategy, all-switches lasts exactly k rounds, switching exactly l_k, l_{k-1}, ..., l_1 in that order.
results.argument: Induction: after r rounds l_{k-r+1..k} continue with value 1; l_{k-r} sees 1 > 1-(k-r)2^{-b}; every l_i with i < k-r sees val(l_{i+1}) = 1-(i+1)2^{-b} < 1-i 2^{-b}.
results.verification: t_lane2.py (and t_lane.py with damping 1/2): k = 3, 5, 8, 12 give N = 13, 24, 43, 64 and exactly k rounds with switch order k,...,1; exact rationals.

results.name: fs14:mixed-objective (side refutation)
results.statement: The objective sum_{Max} x - sum_{Min} x over Q(G) is not minimised at w* in general.
results.argument: Explicit 5-vertex instance Vmin={0,1}, Vmax={2,3}, Vavg={4}, 0->(t1,t1), 1->(2,0), 2->(4,t0), 3->(1,1), 4->(t1,1): minimum -1/2, objective at w* is 0.
results.verification: t_dobj.py: 7 failures on 300 random stopping two-player games, exact LP (mylp.py).

results.name: Quadratic lane-reuse family
results.statement: Sought: a stopping binary SSG family on N = O(k log k) vertices on which Lane(k) is re-run omega(1) times (rounds omega(N)). Not obtained.
results.argument: Re-running the lane needs its exit source and target source to rise alternately by more than the lane's own increment; every design tried (E-chain/T-chain with per-stage loops through the lane, Z-line firing, loop amplifiers with Max or Min gates, tie arming) either had the completion-triggered rise bounded by the completion jump (val_sigma is 1-Lipschitz in a frozen payoff) or relied on closing an intrinsic cycle later than it became attractive, which fs14:cycle forbids. Hill-climbing over one-player binary stopping games (hill.py, n = 12 and 18 non-sinks, 5 seeds, 30-40k mutations each) reached 9 and 11 rounds with at most 4 switches at one vertex.

\subsection{The negative half of the pivot is a published open problem}
\label{sec:fs14}

\begin{proposition}[All-switches on one-player stopping SSGs is Howard's rule on
two-action MDPs]\label{fs14:howard}
Let $G$ be a stopping SSG with $\Vmin=\emptyset$. Then $G$ is, literally, a
transient Markov decision process with exactly two actions per state, whose
reward is $1$ on entering $t_1$ and $0$ otherwise, and for every $\sigma$ the
vector $\val_\sigma$ is the total-reward value of the policy $\sigma$. The
all-switches rule (switch every $v\in\Vmax$ with
$\val_\sigma(\bar\sigma(v))>\val_\sigma(\sigma(v))$, keep ties) is Howard's
greedy policy-iteration rule on that MDP. Consequently a family of stopping
one-player SSGs on $N=m^{O(1)}$ vertices whose all-switches run has
superpolynomial length is an exponential-type lower bound for Howard's
algorithm on two-action MDPs, and conversely any polynomial bound for Howard's
algorithm on two-action transient reachability MDPs bounds the one-player
all-switches run of every stopping SSG.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A Max vertex with its two successors is a state with two deterministic
actions; an average vertex is a state with one action of transition
probabilities $\tfrac12,\tfrac12$; the sinks are absorbing. Stopping means
every policy is transient, so total rewards are finite and equal the
probability of reaching $t_1$, i.e.\ $\val_\sigma$
(\Cref{thm:eval-stopfree}). In an MDP with two actions per state, ``switch
every state that has a switchable action to its most appealing action''
coincides with ``switch every strictly switchable vertex'', since the only
alternative action is the other successor. The two consequences are
restatements.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What is known, and attribution]\label{fs14:literature}
Exponential lower bounds for the all-switches (locally optimising, greedy)
rule are known for parity, mean-payoff, discounted and simple stochastic
games (Friedmann, LMCS 2011, \emph{An exponential lower bound for the latest
deterministic strategy iteration algorithms}) and for Howard's algorithm on
MDPs under the total- and average-reward criteria (Fearnley, ICALP 2010,
\emph{Exponential lower bounds for policy iteration}), and for the simple
reachability objective on MDPs (Christ and Yannakakis, STOC 2023,
\emph{The smoothed complexity of policy iteration for Markov decision
processes}). None of these is binary. In Friedmann's game $G_n$ the vertex
$d_i$ has successors $\{s,e_i,r\}\cup\{a_j:j<2i+1\}$, the vertices $r,s$ have
$n+1$ successors and $k_i$ has $n-i+1$; in Fearnley's MDP the bit state $b_i$
has $2i$ actions into the deceleration lane besides $y$, $x$, the actions to
$f_j$ and the probabilistic action $a_i$, and each lane state $d_k$ has three
actions. The survey sentence of Mukherjee and Kalyanakrishnan (ICAPS 2025,
\emph{Howard's policy iteration is subexponential for deterministic MDPs with
rewards of fixed bit-size and arbitrary discount factor}) is explicit: the
tightest lower bound for Howard's rule on MDPs with a constant number of
actions per state is linear, and ``it remains unknown if exponentially-long
chains are possible for HPI on 2-action MDPs''; the $\Omega(n^2)$ bound of
Hansen and Zwick (2010) is reported there to use $\Theta(n)$ actions per state
as well.
By \Cref{fs14:howard}, the item this document records as missing --- a
stopping SSG family with a superpolynomial all-switches run, equivalently by
\Cref{thm:seed-dichotomy} a family defeating the seeded calculus --- contains
that open problem as its one-player case. Every family constructed in this
document has all-switches length at most $N$, which is the state of the
literature for two actions.
\end{remark}

\subsection{What binary all-switches cannot do: a cycle is active or dead}

The multi-action constructions all time their exponential jumps by
\emph{appeal competition}: in Fearnley's MDP the probabilistic self-loop
$a_i$ has appeal at most $\mathrm{Val}(b_i)+1$ although switching to it lifts
$\mathrm{Val}(b_i)$ to $\mathrm{Val}(g_i)$, which is larger by
$(10n+4)2^{i}$, and the deceleration lane keeps offering $b_i$ actions of
larger appeal for $2i+1$ rounds, after which the greedy rule takes $a_i$.
A binary vertex has no third action to compete with, and the following
one-line consequence of \Cref{cor:comparison} shows that it cannot postpone an
attractive cycle at all.

\begin{lemma}[Dead re-routings]\label{fs14:deadset}
Let $G$ be a stopping SSG, $\sigma$ a Max strategy, and $W\subseteq\Vmax$ a set
of vertices none of which is strictly switchable under $\val_\sigma$, i.e.\
$\val_\sigma(\bar\sigma(v))\le\val_\sigma(\sigma(v))$ for all $v\in W$. Then
$\val_{\sigma[W]}\le\val_\sigma$. Consequently, if
$\sigma=\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\dots$ is any run of strictly improving switches
(single or multiple, all-switches included), then
$\val_{\sigma[W]}\le\val_{\sigma_t}$ for every $t\ge0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At $v\in W$, $(T_{\sigma[W]}\val_\sigma)(v)=\val_\sigma(\bar\sigma(v))\le
\val_\sigma(v)$; at every other vertex $T_{\sigma[W]}$ and $T_\sigma$ agree,
and $T_\sigma\val_\sigma=\val_\sigma$. So $T_{\sigma[W]}\val_\sigma\le\val_\sigma$
and \Cref{cor:comparison} gives $\val_{\sigma[W]}\le\val_\sigma$. For the
second claim it suffices that $\val_{\sigma_{t+1}}\ge\val_{\sigma_t}$ when
$\sigma_{t+1}=\sigma_t[S]$ for a set $S$ of strictly switchable vertices: the
same computation with the inequality reversed gives
$T_{\sigma_t[S]}\val_{\sigma_t}\ge\val_{\sigma_t}$, and \Cref{cor:comparison}
again gives $\val_{\sigma_t[S]}\ge\val_{\sigma_t}$ (for $|S|=1$ this is
\Cref{lem:switch}). Min, if present, best-responds inside $\val_\sigma$
throughout; $T_\sigma$ then carries a minimum at $\Vmin$ and nothing in the
argument changes.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Intrinsic cycle]\label{fs14:intrinsic}
A \emph{cycle} $C=(c_1,\dots,c_k)$ in $G$ is a sequence of Max vertices such
that for each $i$ one successor of $c_i$, its \emph{$C$-option}, leads to
$c_{i+1}$ (indices mod $k$) through average vertices only, every one of which
has its other successor in $\{t_0,t_1\}$ or again on that path. Let
$\sigma\langle C\rangle$ denote any strategy taking the $C$-option at every
$c_i$; the vector $\lambda_C:=\val_{\sigma\langle C\rangle}|_C$ does not depend
on the rest of $\sigma\langle C\rangle$ (from $C$ the play never leaves
$C\cup\{t_0,t_1\}$), and we call it the closed value of $C$. $C$ is
\emph{closed} under $\sigma$ if $\sigma$ takes the $C$-option at every $c_i$,
and \emph{active} under $\sigma$ if some $c_i$ is strictly switchable
\emph{toward} $C$ (its $C$-option is not $\sigma(c_i)$ and
$\val_\sigma(\text{$C$-option})>\val_\sigma(c_i)$).
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[A cycle is active now or dead for ever]\label{fs14:cycle}
Let $G$ be stopping, $C$ an intrinsic cycle and $\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\dots$ a
run of strictly improving switches. If $C$ is not active under $\sigma_t$,
then for every $t'\ge t$: $\val_{\sigma_{t'}}\ge\lambda_C$ on $C$, no vertex of
$C$ is ever again strictly switchable toward $C$ as the last vertex to enter
$C$, and $C$ is closed under $\sigma_{t'}$ only if it was already closed under
$\sigma_t$. In particular, at every round of an all-switches run each intrinsic
cycle either has a vertex switching toward it or will never be closed.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let $W$ be the set of $c_i$ not taking the $C$-option under $\sigma_t$; none is
strictly switchable (toward $C$ is the only alternative), so
\Cref{fs14:deadset} with $\sigma_t[W]=\sigma_t\langle C\rangle$ gives
$\val_{\sigma_{t'}}\ge\lambda_C$ on $C$ for all $t'\ge t$. Suppose $C$ were not
closed under $\sigma_t$ but closed under some $\sigma_{t''}$, $t''>t$ minimal.
The nonempty set $S$ of vertices of $C$ switched toward $C$ in round
$t''-1\to t''$ consists of strictly improving switches, and a strictly
improving switch strictly raises the value of the switched vertex: for $v\in S$,
$\val_{\sigma_{t''}}(v)=\val_{\sigma_{t''}}(\bar\sigma_{t''-1}(v))\ge
\val_{\sigma_{t''-1}}(\bar\sigma_{t''-1}(v))>\val_{\sigma_{t''-1}}(v)$, using
$\val_{\sigma_{t''}}\ge\val_{\sigma_{t''-1}}$. Hence
$\lambda_C(v)=\val_{\sigma_{t''}}(v)>\val_{\sigma_{t''-1}}(v)\ge\lambda_C(v)$, a
contradiction. The last sentence is the contrapositive.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the deceleration-lane counters do not binarise]
\label{fs14:no-arming}
Fearnley's timing needs a vertex whose switch into a cycle would be
improving \emph{now} but is postponed for $2i+1$ rounds by a better competing
action. By \Cref{fs14:cycle} a binary game offers no such state: a cycle whose
closed value exceeds the current values on it has a strictly switchable vertex
every round until it is closed (all-switches starts closing it at once, one
wave of at most $k$ rounds), and a cycle that is once quiet is worth less than
the current values from then on. The amplification the counters rely on ---
a small advantage turned into a jump of order $1/(1-h)$ by a return
probability $h$ close to one (\Cref{thm:impedance} in this document's terms)
--- is therefore available in a binary game only from the first round on, never
after a delay. This is a statement about the mechanism, not a proof that no
binary counter exists; the latter is the open question of
\Cref{fs14:literature}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The binary deceleration lane}

The delay half of the mechanism does binarise, and it is worth recording the
one-line construction because it isolates exactly what is still missing.

\begin{definition}[Lane]\label{fs14:lane-def}
For $k\ge1$ and $b:=\lfloor\log_2 k\rfloor+2$, $\mathrm{Lane}(k)$ has Max vertices
$\ell_1,\dots,\ell_k$ with $\ell_i\to(\ell_{i+1},x_i)$, $\ell_{k+1}:=t_1$, where
$x_i$ is a coin of value $1-i2^{-b}$ realised by a chain of $b$ average
vertices (\Cref{lem:gadget}). It is stopping, one-player, has $N\le k(b+1)+2=
O(k\log k)$ vertices, and all its values are dyadic with $b$ bits.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[One switch per round]\label{fs14:lane}
From the strategy $\sigma_0$ that exits everywhere, the all-switches run on
$\mathrm{Lane}(k)$ lasts exactly $k$ rounds and switches exactly one vertex per
round, in the order $\ell_k,\ell_{k-1},\dots,\ell_1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Under $\sigma_0$, $\val(\ell_i)=1-i2^{-b}$. Induction on the round $r\ge0$:
under $\sigma_r$ the vertices $\ell_{k-r+1},\dots,\ell_k$ continue and have value
$1$, the others exit. Then $\ell_{k-r}$ is strictly switchable
($1>1-(k-r)2^{-b}$), while for $i<k-r$ the continue option is worth
$\val(\ell_{i+1})=1-(i+1)2^{-b}<1-i2^{-b}$. So exactly $\ell_{k-r}$ switches.
After round $k$ no vertex is switchable and the run halts.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Verification, and the exact gap]\label{fs14:gap}
\Cref{fs14:deadset} was checked in exact rational arithmetic on $250$ random
stopping games ($152$ with both players), all $1202$ re-routings of up to
three non-switchable vertices being dominated by every later value vector of
the all-switches run; \Cref{fs14:cycle} on random games built around random
intrinsic cycles of length $2$--$4$ with random masses and pass probabilities
($150$ runs, $272$ inactive (round, cycle) events, no violation);
\Cref{fs14:lane} for $k=3,5,8,12$ ($N=13,24,43,64$), the
switch order being $k,k-1,\dots,1$ each time. A hill-climbing search over
one-player binary stopping games with $n=12$ and $n=18$ non-sinks, maximising
the all-switches length, reached $9$ and $11$ rounds respectively with at most
$4$ switches at any single vertex --- consistent with the linear state of the
art. What is missing, stated exactly: a stopping binary SSG family on
$N=O(k\log k)$ vertices in which the lane of \Cref{fs14:lane} is re-run
$\omega(1)$ times. Re-running it requires the exit source and the target
source to rise alternately by more than the lane's own increment; in every
design tried here the rise triggered by a completion was bounded by that
increment (a switch that was non-improving before the trigger gains at most
what its option gained, since $\val_\sigma$ is $1$-Lipschitz in a frozen
payoff), or the structure meant to amplify it was an intrinsic cycle, which by
\Cref{fs14:cycle} closes as soon as it is worth closing.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[A side refutation]\label{fs14:mixed-objective}
The objective $\sum_{v\in\Vmax}x(v)-\sum_{v\in\Vmin}x(v)$ over $Q(G)$ is not
minimised at $w^\ast$ in general: on $300$ random stopping games with both
players it failed on $7$, e.g.\ $\Vmin=\{0,1\}$, $\Vmax=\{2,3\}$, $\Vavg=\{4\}$,
$0\to(t_1,t_1)$, $1\to(2,0)$, $2\to(4,t_0)$, $3\to(1,1)$, $4\to(t_1,1)$, where
the minimum is $-\tfrac12$ while the objective at $w^\ast$ is $0$. So the one objective
that treats the two players symmetrically does not escape
\Cref{thm:transport-objective}.
\end{remark}
